definition.text: A large land or water area defined by its environmental resources and containing a geographically distinct assemblage of natural communities and species.

facts.text: WWF's definition requires that communities share most of their species and dynamics, share similar environmental conditions, and interact ecologically in ways critical to their long-term persistence.
Boundaries rarely form abrupt edges; they are bounded by ecotones and mosaic habitats, and most ecoregions contain habitats that differ from their assigned biome.
Bailey's algorithmic system gives priority to climate and ecological criteria; the WWF system, built for biodiversity conservation planning, gives priority to the distribution of species assemblages.
The WWF framework first set out 867 terrestrial ecoregions in 14 biomes and 8 biogeographic realms; a 2017 update with satellite imagery reduced the count to 846 and later 844.
Marine ecoregions of the world number 232, grouped into 62 provinces and 12 realms; the freshwater map of 2008 has 426 ecoregions.
The Global 200 is WWF's list of priority ecoregions for conservation.

definition.text: A minor atmospheric gas that is an active part of the planetary nitrogen cycle and a long-lived greenhouse gas.

facts.text: It is the third most important greenhouse gas for global warming and has been a major ozone-depleting substance.

Per molecule over 100 years it traps 265 times as much heat as CO2, but its concentration is under one thousandth of CO2's, so its greenhouse contribution is less than one third that of carbon dioxide.
Atmospheric abundance has grown more than 20% from about 270 ppb in 1750, surpassing 330 ppb in 2017, and is rising about 1 ppb per year.
About 40% of emissions are human-caused, with growth chiefly from expanding agriculture; annual human emissions equal about 3 billion tonnes of CO2 in greenhouse effect.
Microbes produce it by nitrification, denitrification and nitrifier denitrification.
